newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu warns PLO not to declare state.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu warns PLO not to declare state.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Monday warned President Yasser Arafat, bouyed by the PLO's entry into Hebron, not to declare a Palestinian state in the West Bank and Gaza Strip.
Netanyahu spoke as two more Israeli-Palestinian patrols began rounds in the town of Hebron, a long-time West Bank flashpoint for Jewish-Arab violence.

Asked by Israel Radio how he would react to a unilateral declaration of Palestinian statehood, Netanyahu said: "If there is a one-sided declaration by the Palestinians concerning the final agreement...we will respond very severely.
"This would be a violation of the agreement."

Arafat received a hero's welcome in Hebron on Sunday, telling thousands of cheering Palestinians that the latest peace deal with Israel was a "springboard for what comes after...so that we can establish our independent Palestinian state."

Israel and the PLO signed a Hebron deal last week after months of negotiations and arm-twisting by the United States. By Friday, Israel had withdrawn its troops from most of the town, concentrating them in Jewish enclaves where 400 settlers live in the heart of Hebron.
The Hebron deal is part of several interim agreements reached since 1993 that have given self-rule to much of the Palestinian population of the West Bank and Gaza Strip.
The final status of these areas, which Israel captured in the 1967 Middle East war, is to be determined in negotiations ending no later than May 1999.
Arafat views Palestinian statehood as the natural culmination of final-status talks while Netanyahu rejects the establishment of a Palestinian state, saying statehood could endanger Israel.
However, Arafat did not threaten in Hebron to unilaterally declare a Palestinian state, focusing on the success of a peace process he hopes will produce independence.
In a sign that months of frosty relations between the two leaders may be thawing, Netanyahu said on Monday there was a new tone to Arafat's remarks.
"We welcome the more positive tone. This is a better direction," Netanyahu told Israel Radio.

Jewish residents of Hebron say the accord threatens their existence because Palestinian police could turn their guns on settlers. Four joint Israeli-Palestinian patrols were touring Hebron on Monday under terms of the agreement.

The Hebron accord, the first agreement with the PLO signed by Netanyahu's right-wing Likud party, also outlines further withdrawals Israeli troops are to make from parts of the West Bank beginning on March 7.
But Netanyahu told Israel's army radio the deal ensured that Israel alone would determine the scope of subsequent redeployments.
"We will define the areas we need for maintaining our security and this is also agreed upon by the Americans -- that the side which will determine the scope of redeployments is Israel," he said.

Palestinians say Israel should withdraw troops from at least 90 percent of the West Bank and Gaza by the time of the final redeployment in mid-1998. Israeli officials say it is too early to determine how much its troops will vacate.
